alignment.note: Greek uses neuter predicate adjective καλὸν τὸ ἅλας with article; Peshitta employs feminine predicate adjective ܫܦܝܪܐ ܗܝ ܡܠܚܐ with copula pronoun ܗܝ, reflecting Syriac grammatical gender conventions for ܡܠܚܐ (feminine).

Greek employs the adjective ἄναλον ('unsalty, saltless') with the verb γένηται ('become') to express loss of savor. Peshitta substitutes the verb ܬܦܟܗ ('it becomes insipid, loses flavor'), a lexical choice that collapses the Greek adjective-verb construction into a single verbal predicate.

Greek uses prepositional phrase ἐν τίνι ('with what') followed by object pronoun αὐτὸ and verb ἀρτύσετε ('will you season'); Peshitta employs instrumental ܒܡܢܐ ('with what') directly followed by the verb ܬܬܡܠܚ ('will it be salted'), omitting an explicit object pronoun as the verb's morphology encodes the subject.

Greek imperative ἔχετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἅλα ('have salt in yourselves') uses a prepositional phrase with reflexive pronoun. Peshitta renders with jussive ܬܗܘܐ ܒܟܘܢ ܡܠܚܐ ('let there be salt in you'), employing an existential construction with second-person plural pronominal suffix rather than a reflexive.

Greek uses reciprocal pronoun ἀλλήλοις ('one another') with preposition ἐν. Peshitta employs the idiomatic distributive construction ܚܕ ܥܡ ܚܕ ('one with one'), a standard Syriac rendering of reciprocal relationships, semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct.
